entityDossier.whatItIs: A joint hearing of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability's Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation and its Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, titled 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth,' held 13 November 2024 at 11:30 a.m. in 2154 Rayburn House Office Building. The four witnesses were Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet USN (Ret.), Luis Elizondo, Michael Gold, and Michael Shellenberger. Written testimony from all four is published on the committee's website.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the hearing that entered the name of an alleged active Unacknowledged Special Access Program — IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION — into the congressional record, together with the sourced allegation that the program is controlled by the White House and executed by DoD specifically 'to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code.' It is also the hearing at which a retired flag officer testified under his own name that a UAP safety-of-flight email was deleted from Navy accounts overnight, and at which a former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program for the White House and NSC testified that 'the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies.' The same witness testified that the Pentagon's Public Affairs Office employs a psychological operations officer as the single point of contact for UAP inquiries, and another witness described being subjected to an hours-long influence operation by the then-acting AARO director. The hearing converts whistleblower assertions into dated, attributable, congressionally-published documents.
entityDossier.narrative:
The November 2024 hearing was the third in the House Oversight sequence that began with the July 2023 Grusch hearing, and it is the one that matters most structurally, because it moved the argument from 'there are unexplained objects' to 'there is a named program and a named legal evasion.'

Michael Shellenberger's written testimony carries the load. He reported that a current or former US government official acting as a whistleblower had written a report, provided to authorised committees of Congress and their staff, stating that 'the Executive Branch has been managing UAP/NHI issues without Congressional knowledge, oversight, or authorization for some time, quite possibly decades.' The report names an active DoD Unacknowledged Special Access Program, IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION, described by the document's source as a 'strategic intelligence program' that is part of the military's family of long-standing highly-sensitive programs dealing with aspects of the UAP problem. The report states that 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION serves as a central or parent USAP that consolidates observations' of UAP 'by both tasked and untasked collection platforms,' and that it 'includes high-quality Imagery Intelligence (IMINT) and Measurement and Signature Intelligence (MASINT) of UAPs,' sourced from a blend of directed and incidental collection in Low Earth Orbit, the upper atmosphere, aviation altitudes and maritime environments. The whistleblower alleges the USAP was created in 2017, after the New York Times published its AATIP story.

The program's stated function, as quoted in the testimony, is the concealment mechanism itself: 'the existence of IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION demonstrates the extant capability to detect, quarantine, and transfer UAP and RV [Reproduction Vehicle] collection incidents before they are observed and circulated within the Military Intelligence Enterprise, thus serving as a means of enforcing internal information security.' That is a claim about a filter operating upstream of the intelligence enterprise, and it is the single most consequential sentence in the hearing record.

The legal mechanism follows. DoD spokesperson Sue Gough issued a categorical denial: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION.' After publication, Shellenberger says a source told him the SAP 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code' — 'It is essentially a DOD Program, as the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.' A former IC official told him: 'That program is run out of SEC DEF. They don't want to acknowledge it's real.' Shellenberger also notes that AARO is housed within OUSD(I&S), so 'the office that Congress created to investigate unreported UAP programs is troublingly close to the organizations running the alleged programs.' A source warned him that merely printing the program name could trigger FISA surveillance of whoever published it.

The testimony also describes two incidents from the whistleblower's report. An F-22 'broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs,' with one holding station within twelve metres starboard of the cockpit, 'maintaining its exact position and orientation parallel with the F-22's cockpit despite multiple evasive rolls and maneuvers,' the aircraft then 'forced out of the mission area under the escort of the UAP formation.' Separately, an aircraft carrier's crew observed a 'small orange-red sphere' descend to 100-200 yards above the flight deck, emitting light that 'did not illuminate the ocean or the flight deck of the CVN despite the visual appearance of intense luminosity,' with a surface 'roiling like the surface of the sun.'

Tim Gallaudet's testimony supplies the institutional-deletion evidence. In January 2015, as Commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, he received an email on the Navy's secure network from the Fleet Forces Command operations officer, addressed to all subordinate commanders, subject line in capitals: 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE,' attaching what is now the 'Go Fast' video. 'The very next day, the email disappeared from my account and those of the other recipients without explanation,' and neither the Commander of Fleet Forces nor his operations officer ever raised it again. Gallaudet's inference is stated plainly: 'I concluded that the UAP information must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' He further testified that in 2024 he was the object of an hours-long influence operation by the then-acting AARO director and senior staff, aimed at validating AARO's historical records report, questioning the Nimitz tic tac case, and disparaging former officials who have spoken publicly. He told the committee that on 11 November 2024, two days before the hearing, Chris Mellon had asked for his help getting Congress details of a 2017 case involving satellite imagery of UAP 'that has still not been shared with Congress.'

Luis Elizondo's testimony is the shortest and the most direct: 'UAP are real. Advanced technologies not made by our Government — or any other government — are monitoring sensitive military installations around the globe. Furthermore, the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies, as are some of our adversaries. I believe we are in the midst of a multi-decade, secretive arms race — one funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from our elected representatives and oversight bodies.' He established his standing in the same paragraph: 'In my last position, I managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council.' He described a 'small cadre' inside government that has created 'a culture of suppression and intimidation,' including 'unwarranted criminal investigations, harassment, and efforts to destroy one's credibility,' and stated that many of his former colleagues have given classified testimony to the DoD and Intelligence Community Inspectors General and were subsequently targeted with threats to their careers, clearances 'and even our lives.'

Michael Gold's testimony is the counterweight in tone but not in direction: a former NASA associate administrator arguing that stigma, not evidence, is the binding constraint.

What the record does not settle: no committee has published the underlying Immaculate Constellation report, no dates or units are attached to the F-22 or carrier incidents, and the acting AARO director in Gallaudet's account is not named in his written testimony.

claims.text: The hearing 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth' was held 13 November 2024 at 11:30 a.m. in 2154 Rayburn House Office Building, jointly by the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation and the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs.

The four witnesses were Dr. Tim Gallaudet (Rear Admiral, USN Ret., CEO of Ocean STL Consulting LLC), Luis Elizondo (author and former DoD official), Michael Gold (former NASA Associate Administrator for Space Policy and Partnerships and member of the NASA UAP Independent Study Team), and Michael Shellenberger (founder of Public).

Luis Elizondo testified: 'UAP are real. Advanced technologies not made by our Government – or any other government – are monitoring sensitive military installations around the globe. Furthermore, the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies, as are some of our adversaries.'
Elizondo testified: 'In my last position, I managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council.'

Elizondo testified that 'the Pentagon's very own Public Affairs Office openly employs a professional psychological operations officer as the singular point of contact for any UAP-related inquiries from citizens and the media.'

Gallaudet testified that in January 2015, as Commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, he received an email on the Navy's secure network from the Fleet Forces Command operations officer with the subject line 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' attaching the 'Go Fast' video, and that 'the very next day, the email disappeared from my account and those of the other recipients without explanation.'

Gallaudet testified: 'I concluded that the UAP information must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency — a compartmented program that even senior officials, including myself, were not read into.'

Gallaudet testified that during a 2024 meeting with the then-acting AARO director and his senior staff he 'was the object of an hours-long influence operation' aimed at validating AARO's historical records report, questioning the USS Nimitz 'tic tac' encounter, and disparaging former government authorities who have spoken publicly about US government UAP programs.

Gallaudet testified that on 11 November 2024 former DoD official Chris Mellon contacted him seeking assistance in sharing with Congress details of a 2017 case involving satellite imagery of UAP 'that has still not been shared with Congress,' and offered to provide the dates in a closed setting.

Shellenberger's written testimony states that a whistleblower report provided to authorised committees of Congress names an active DoD Unacknowledged Special Access Program called IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION which 'serves as a central or parent USAP that consolidates observations' of UAP 'by both tasked and untasked collection platforms,' and that the Executive Branch 'has been managing UAP/NHI issues without Congressional knowledge, oversight, or authorization for some time, quite possibly decades.'
Shellenberger's testimony quotes DoD spokesperson Sue Gough: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION."'

Shellenberger testified that after publication a source told him the SAP 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code,' adding: 'It is essentially a DOD Program, as the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.' A former IC official separately told him 'That program is run out of SEC DEF... They don't want to acknowledge it's real.'

The whistleblower report quoted in the testimony concludes that 'the existence of IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION demonstrates the extant capability to detect, quarantine, and transfer UAP and RV [Reproduction Vehicle] collection incidents before they are observed and circulated within the Military Intelligence Enterprise, thus serving as a means of enforcing internal information security.'

Shellenberger's testimony notes that AARO is housed within the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, so 'the office that Congress created to investigate unreported UAP programs is troublingly close to the organizations running the alleged programs,' and that a source warned him that printing the program name 'could trigger government surveillance of me under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act.'

The whistleblower report describes an F-22 that 'broke trajectory and attempted to evade but was intercepted and boxed in by approximately 3-6 UAPs,' one of which held station within twelve metres starboard of the cockpit maintaining exact position and orientation through multiple evasive rolls, the aircraft being 'forced out of the mission area under the escort of the UAP formation'; and a carrier incident in which an orange-red sphere descended to 100-200 yards above the flight deck emitting light that 'did not illuminate the ocean or the flight deck of the CVN,' its surface 'roiling like the surface of the sun.'

Gallaudet's testimony asserts a constitutional argument: 'Even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight, and all compartmented programs must be reported to the Senate Intelligence Committee. Any and all past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs and activities are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress.'

entityDossier.denialPosture: DoD spokesperson Sue Gough issued a categorical, attributable denial quoted into the hearing record: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION.' The denial is framed as a records statement rather than a factual one, and is exactly the form of denial the alleged White-House-controlled, DoD-executed structure would produce.
connections: Chairwoman Nancy Mace (Cybersecurity, IT and Government Innovation) and Chairman Glenn Grothman (National Security, the Border and Foreign Affairs) presided, with Ranking Members Gerald Connolly and Robert Garcia — all four named in each witness's opening address.

IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION is alleged to have been created in 2017 in response to the 16 December 2017 New York Times AATIP article, making that article the causal trigger for a new concealment structure.
The alleged Title 10 evasion — White House direction, SECDEF execution — is a claim about 10 U.S.C. 119 specifically, and about the SAP governance chain set out in DoDD 5205.07.

AARO's placement inside OUSD(I&S) puts the investigating office inside the same organisation that DoDD 5205.07 designates as the primary DoD interface to ODNI and the IC for shared compartmented capabilities.
Chris Mellon's 2017 satellite-imagery case, raised two days before the hearing, is an unresolved thread linking the hearing to national technical means and to whichever agency holds that imagery.

Gallaudet's January 2015 email connects the hearing to the USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group pre-deployment exercise and to the 'Go Fast' video, and by extension to Fleet Forces Command's leadership at the time.

Elizondo's account of colleagues giving classified testimony to the DoD and IC Inspectors General links this hearing to the ICIG channel through which David Grusch's 2022 complaint was found credible and urgent.

Michael Gold connects the hearing to NASA (Bill Nelson, Thomas Zurbuchen, Daniel Evans, the UAP Independent Study Team) and to Redwire Space, where he is Chief Growth Officer and where fellow IST member Reggie Brothers sits on the board.
Gallaudet's advisory roles link the hearing to the Sol Foundation, the UAP Disclosure Fund, Harvard's Galileo Project, and Ryan Graves's Americans for Safe Aerospace.
openQuestions: Who is the IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION whistleblower, and did any committee formally obtain and retain the underlying report?
What dates, units and locations attach to the F-22 encounter and the carrier flight-deck sphere described in the report?
Who was the acting AARO director present at the meeting Gallaudet describes as an influence operation, and who were the senior staff?
Was Chris Mellon's 2017 satellite-imagery case ever briefed to the oversight committees, and which agency holds the imagery?
Did DoD's denial address only the exact string 'IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION,' and would a nickname change or an unacknowledged compartment render the denial technically accurate?
Is there a written record of the Fleet Forces Command email Gallaudet describes, and was its deletion a routine recall or a directed action?

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence is the coordinating headquarters of the US Intelligence Community, created by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 and headed by the Director of National Intelligence. Since 2021 it has been the statutory co-owner of the government's UAP reporting machinery: it published the June 2021 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' it is the office with which the Secretary of Defense must coordinate in establishing and running AARO, and it co-issues the annual consolidated UAP reports. Its Inspector General is also the channel through which UAP whistleblower complaints reach the congressional intelligence committees.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: ODNI sits on both sides of the ledger, and that is precisely what makes it useful. It is the office that publicly certified that most reported UAP 'probably do represent physical objects,' that eleven documented pilot near-misses exist, and — critically — that it could not confirm that any of the collected reports were attributable to classified US government or industry developmental programs. An intelligence headquarters that cannot deconflict a UAP dataset against its own black programs is either not being told, or is telling us it is not being told. At the same time, ODNI is the institutional counterparty for every DoD SAP that shares compartmented capabilities with the IC, and AARO is lodged inside the DoD office designated as ODNI's primary interface. Its Inspector General found David Grusch's complaint alleging concealed retrieval and reverse-engineering programs 'credible and urgent' and forwarded it to the DNI and both intelligence committees, after which nothing publicly followed. Even the FOIA-released version of its own 2021 assessment is redacted under (b)(1) and (b)(3), including the identity of the official it names as accountable.
entityDossier.narrative:
ODNI's formal entry into the UAP file came through an appropriations rider rather than through the intelligence community's own initiative. Senate Report 116-233, accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, directed the DNI, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, to submit an intelligence assessment of the threat posed by unidentified aerial phenomena and of the progress the Department of Defense Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force had made in understanding it. The resulting nine-page unclassified 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena,' dated 25 June 2021, is the single most-cited government document on the subject, and it repays close reading of the FOIA copy rather than the sanitised public one.

The drafting roster alone is analytically valuable. The report was 'drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and ODNI/National Intelligence Council.' That is a list of every organisation with an equity in the file as of 2021, and it is a map of where records exist.

The substantive findings are hedged but not empty. 'Most of the UAP reported probably do represent physical objects given that a majority of UAP registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation.' The UAPTF 'has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.' The dataset is limited primarily to US government reporting of incidents from November 2004 to March 2021. The report proposes five explanatory bins — airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or US industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other' — and then, on the third bin, delivers the sentence a program hypothesis must build on: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to classified USG aerospace programs or systems under development by commercial aerospace firms. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.' On foreign adversaries: 'We currently lack data to determine any UAP are part of a foreign collection program or indicative of a major technological advancement by a potential adversary.' On collection: 'The UAPTF had no MASINT reporting on the events considered in this dataset' — which stands in direct tension with the later Immaculate Constellation allegation that a parent USAP holds high-quality IMINT and MASINT of UAP.

The redaction pattern is itself evidence. The FOIA version, approved for release on 24 March 2022 under case DF-2021-00275, still withholds material under (b)(1) — properly classified national defence information — and (b)(3), statutory exemption. The sentence identifying the accountable official reads, in the released copy, 'The UAPTF Director, is the official accountable for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP,' with the name removed. Passages describing unusual flight characteristics, GEOINT and SIGINT collection, and specific incidents are blank. The unclassified public product is therefore a curated fraction of what Congress received, and the delta is where the argument lives.

ODNI's second role is structural. Under 50 U.S.C. 3373 the Secretary of Defense must act 'in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence' in establishing AARO, and the reporting mechanism must be established 'in consultation with the Director of National Intelligence.' AARO is housed inside OUSD(I&S). And DoDD 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, designates USD(I&S) as the office that 'serves as the primary interface for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and members of the Intelligence Community (IC), including sharing with the DoD compartmented capabilities and information intended for inclusion and subsequent apportionment.' In other words, the same office that hosts the body Congress created to find unreported UAP programs is the office through which IC compartmented capabilities are moved into and out of DoD special access programs. Whether that is an oversight design flaw or the point is the question the board exists to press.

The third role is the whistleblower channel. In 2022, while at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, David Grusch filed a Presidential Policy Directive 19 urgent-concern complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General. Thomas Monheim, IC Inspector General from April 2020 to January 2025, found the complaint credible and urgent, and a summary went to the Director of National Intelligence and to the House and Senate intelligence committees. Grusch then testified publicly to House Oversight in July 2023. No ODNI product has since publicly addressed the substance of the referral.

Finally, ODNI has been the co-publisher of record for the successor reporting. The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, released 14 November 2024 the day after the House Oversight hearing, reported 757 UAP reports received, 485 of which occurred within the reporting period and 272 of which occurred in 2021-2022 but were reported late; 118 cases resolved to prosaic objects; 21 unresolved. That report is a DoD/AARO product carried on the ODNI website, and under this board's sourcing rules it is a primary record of what the government said, not of what is true.

What the record does not show is any ODNI statement about retrievals, materials, or reverse-engineering. There is no ODNI acknowledgement of a legacy program, and no public ODNI response to the Grusch referral.

claims.text: The 25 June 2021 'Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena' was produced by ODNI in response to a provision in Senate Report 116-233 accompanying the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, directing the DNI in consultation with the Secretary of Defense to assess the threat posed by UAP and the UAPTF's progress.

The assessment states it 'was drafted by the UAPTF and the ODNI National Intelligence Manager for Aviation, with input from USD(I&S), DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, Air Force, Army, Navy, Marine Corps, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, ODNI/NIM-Emerging and Disruptive Technology, ODNI/National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and ODNI/National Intelligence Council.'

The assessment states: 'Most of the UAP reported probably do represent physical objects given that a majority of UAP registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation.'
The assessment states: 'The UAPTF has 11 reports of documented instances in which pilots reported near misses with a UAP.'

On the possibility that UAP are US black programs the assessment states: 'Some UAP observations could be attributable to classified USG aerospace programs or systems under development by commercial aerospace firms. We were unable to confirm, however, that these systems accounted for any of the UAP reports we collected.'
The assessment states: 'The UAPTF had no MASINT reporting on the events considered in this dataset.'

The assessment defines five explanatory categories into which resolved UAP incidents would fall: airborne clutter, natural atmospheric phenomena, USG or U.S. industry developmental programs, foreign adversary systems, and a catchall 'other' bin.
The dataset described in the assessment 'is currently limited primarily to USG reporting of incidents occurring from November 2004 to March 2021.'

The FOIA-released version of the assessment, approved for release by ODNI on 24 March 2022 under case DF-2021-00275, withholds material under exemptions (b)(1) and (b)(3), including the name of the UAPTF Director identified in the text as 'the official accountable for ensuring the timely collection and consolidation of data on UAP,' redacted under (b)(3) and (b)(6).
The assessment notes 'some UAP have been detected near military facilities or by aircraft carrying the USG's most advanced sensor systems.'

DoD Directive 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, designates USD(I&S) as the office that 'serves as the primary interface for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and members of the Intelligence Community (IC), including sharing with the DoD compartmented capabilities and information intended for inclusion and subsequent apportionment' — the same office in which AARO is housed.

50 U.S.C. 3373 requires the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, to establish the office known as the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, and requires the secure UAP reporting mechanism to be established in consultation with the DNI.

In 2022 Intelligence Community Inspector General Thomas Monheim found David Grusch's PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint credible and urgent, and a summary was transmitted to the Director of National Intelligence and to the House and Senate intelligence committees; Grusch subsequently testified publicly to House Oversight in July 2023.

Michael Shellenberger's November 2024 congressional testimony quotes DNI John Ratcliffe stating in 2021 that UAP demonstrated 'technologies that we don't have and, frankly, that we are not capable of defending against,' that analysts had 'high confidence' foreign adversaries were not behind the Tic Tac encounter, and that 'there are a lot more sightings than have been made public.'

The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, released 14 November 2024 and carried on the ODNI website, reports 757 UAP reports received, of which 485 occurred within the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were reported late; 118 cases were resolved to prosaic objects and 21 remain unexplained.

Sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, now codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, require NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection consisting of 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence'; NARA established Record Group 615 for it, creating a statutory transfer obligation that reaches every IC element ODNI coordinates.

entityDossier.denialPosture: ODNI has never denied that a legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering program exists; it has denied confirmation. Its 2021 assessment states it was 'unable to confirm' that US classified aerospace programs accounted for any collected UAP report, and that it 'currently lacks data' to attribute UAP to a foreign collection program. The characteristic ODNI posture is epistemic hedging plus redaction, not categorical denial — which is a materially different artifact from the flat DoD denials on this board.
connections: ODNI to UAPTF to AARO: the same reporting lineage, with ODNI's National Intelligence Manager for Aviation as the drafting office in 2021 and AARO now lodged inside OUSD(I&S), ODNI's designated DoD interface under DoDD 5205.07.

The 2021 drafting roster names every agency with a UAP equity as of that date — DIA, FBI, NRO, NGA, NSA, DARPA, FAA, NASA, NOAA, NCSC, NIC — and is therefore a target list for NARA Record Group 615 transfer compliance.
The redacted UAPTF Director's name under (b)(6) is a specific, resolvable identity gap; the same office is the accountability node the Senate report demanded be identified.

ICIG Thomas Monheim to DNI Avril Haines to the congressional intelligence committees is the documented Grusch referral path; the substance of what ODNI did with it is unaddressed in any public product.

The assessment's statement that the UAPTF had no MASINT reporting sits in direct conflict with the Immaculate Constellation allegation that a parent USAP holds high-quality IMINT and MASINT — either the UAPTF was walled off from that collection, or one of the two statements is false.

DNI John Ratcliffe's 2021 public statements are the most permissive on-record remarks by any DNI and are quoted into the congressional record by a November 2024 witness; DNI succession since (Haines, Gabbard, Clayton) is a change-of-posture axis worth tracking.
Michael Gold's testimony connects ODNI's collection problem to NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System and to CNES/GEIPAN as civil-side data sources the IC has not integrated.
openQuestions: Who is the UAPTF Director redacted under (b)(6) in the FOIA copy of the 2021 assessment?
What does the classified annex to the 2021 preliminary assessment contain, and who at ODNI has seen it?
What action, if any, did ODNI or the DNI take on the ICIG's credible-and-urgent referral of the Grusch complaint?
Has ODNI or any IC element transferred records to NARA Record Group 615, and what did they withhold?
Which ODNI element holds equity in any UAP-related compartmented capability shared with DoD SAPs through the USD(I&S) interface?
Why could the IC not deconflict its own UAP dataset against classified US aerospace programs — was the deconfliction attempted and refused, or never possible at the UAPTF's access level?

entityDossier.whatItIs: 'Glowing Auras and "Black Money": The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program,' a New York Times article published 16 December 2017 by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal and Leslie Kean. It revealed the existence of the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, its $22 million funding, its origin at the request of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, and its management by Luis Elizondo from the fifth floor of the Pentagon's C Ring. It was accompanied by the release of US Navy FLIR gun-camera footage.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the date on which the concealment failed in public, and the article says so in its own lede: $22 million inside a $600 billion budget 'was almost impossible to find. Which was how the Pentagon wanted it.' The piece establishes three facts the program argument rests on: that the Defense Department had never before acknowledged the program's existence, that DoD said it shut down in 2012, and that the program's own backers said it did not — that officials continued to investigate episodes for five more years while carrying out other duties. That is a documented, contemporaneous dispute about whether a UAP program continued to run after the government said it had stopped. Every subsequent institutional response — the UAP Task Force, the 2021 ODNI assessment, AARO, the 2023 and 2024 hearings, the NARA records collection — is downstream of this article, and a whistleblower report given to Congress in 2024 alleges that a new Unacknowledged Special Access Program was created in 2017 in direct response to it.
entityDossier.narrative:
The article is short on speculation and long on institutional fact, which is why it has held up. Its reporting basis is stated in the second paragraph: the program was documented 'according to Defense Department officials, interviews with program participants and records obtained by The New York Times.' Three sourcing streams, one of them documentary. Those records have never been published in full, and their contents remain one of the most valuable unexploited leads on the board.

The factual core is compact. The Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program was funded at $22 million within Defense Department budgets of roughly $600 billion a year. It was run by Luis Elizondo, a military intelligence official, from the fifth floor of the Pentagon's C Ring. The Defense Department had never previously acknowledged that it existed. DoD said it shut the program down in 2012. And — the sentence that does the most work — 'its backers say that, while the Pentagon ended funding for the effort at that time, the program remains in existence. For the past five years, they say, officials with the program have continued to investigate episodes brought to them by service members, while also carrying out their other Defense Department duties.'

That construction is the whole concealment argument in miniature. A program is funded through a line item that is hard to find. Its existence is not acknowledged. When it becomes inconvenient, funding is ended and the government says the program is over. The work continues anyway, distributed across officials' other duties, which is exactly the arrangement that makes a program invisible to the reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. 119 — there is no new SAP to notify, no budget line to report, and no milestone schedule to submit. Whether that is what happened is not proven by the article. What the article proves is that people with direct knowledge asserted it on the record in December 2017, and that DoD's contrary position was already a matter of dispute at the moment of first disclosure.

The money trail the article opened has been independently corroborated by the government's own subsequent releases. Steven Aftergood, writing for the Federation of American Scientists in January 2019 on the occasion of DIA's FOIA release of the 38 funded research titles, described the same program in the same terms: 'From 2007 to 2012, the DIA spent $22 million on the activity, formally known as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program. It was apparently initiated at the behest of then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, with most of the funding directed to a Nevada constituent of his' — and cited this article by name. The Debrief's 2021 investigation into BAASS likewise anchors its $22 million figure to this piece. So the article's central financial claim has been ratified by a FOIA release, by an arms-control watchdog, and by a subsequent investigative outlet using different documents.

The article's second, less-discussed effect was on the evidentiary record itself. It carried Navy infrared gun-camera footage into mainstream circulation, which the Navy later confirmed as authentic imagery of unidentified aerial phenomena. That transformed the subject from a testimony problem into a sensor-data problem, and it is the reason later official documents — including the 2021 ODNI assessment's observation that a majority of UAP 'registered across multiple sensors, to include radar, infrared, electro-optical, weapon seekers, and visual observation' — are framed in terms of instrumentation rather than eyewitnesses.

The third effect is the one that matters most for this board, and it is alleged rather than established. In written testimony to House Oversight on 13 November 2024, Michael Shellenberger reported that a whistleblower's report provided to congressional committees alleges that DoD created an Unacknowledged Special Access Program called IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION in 2017, after this article was published, to serve as a 'central or parent USAP' consolidating UAP observations and enforcing internal information security by detecting, quarantining and transferring collection incidents before they circulate within the Military Intelligence Enterprise. If true, this article did not merely expose a program — it caused a new and better-hidden one. DoD spokesperson Sue Gough has denied that any SAP by that name exists in its records.

There are also unresolved discrepancies that a careful analyst should hold onto. The article and FAS both date the program 2007-2012 and call it AATIP; the DIA contracting record dates the BAASS contract to 2008 and calls the effort AAWSAP; Shellenberger's testimony dates AAWSAP 2009-2017 with reports ending in 2010 and the program running through 2012. The government has never issued a clean, consistent account of the relationship between AATIP and AAWSAP, and that inconsistency is not incidental — it is the kind of ambiguity that survives only when nobody is compelled to resolve it.

What the article does not do: it does not allege retrievals, materials, or reverse-engineering. It does not name a contractor in its lede. Its claims about the program's survival past 2012 are attributed to unnamed backers, and its documentary basis has never been made public.

claims.text: 'Glowing Auras and "Black Money": The Pentagon's Mysterious U.F.O. Program' was published by The New York Times on 16 December 2017 and written by Helene Cooper, Ralph Blumenthal and Leslie Kean.

The article opens: 'In the $600 billion annual Defense Department budgets, the $22 million spent on the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program was almost impossible to find. Which was how the Pentagon wanted it.'
The article states the program 'was run by a military intelligence official, Luis Elizondo, on the fifth floor of the Pentagon's C Ring, deep within the building's maze.'

The article states: 'The Defense Department has never before acknowledged the existence of the program, which it says it shut down in 2012. But its backers say that, while the Pentagon ended funding for the effort at that time, the program remains in existence.'

The article states: 'For the past five years, they say, officials with the program have continued to investigate episodes brought to them by service members, while also carrying out their other Defense Department duties.'

The article's stated evidentiary basis is 'Defense Department officials, interviews with program participants and records obtained by The New York Times'; those records have never been published in full.

The Federation of American Scientists, writing in January 2019 on the DIA's FOIA release of 38 funded research titles, corroborated that 'from 2007 to 2012, the DIA spent $22 million on the activity, formally known as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program' and that it was 'apparently initiated at the behest of then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, with most of the funding directed to a Nevada constituent of his,' citing this article by name.
The Debrief's January 2021 investigation into BAASS anchors the $22 million DIA-to-Bigelow figure directly to this New York Times article.

Michael Shellenberger testified to House Oversight on 13 November 2024 that a whistleblower alleges DoD created the Unacknowledged Special Access Program IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION in 2017 'after the New York Times published an article describing an informal Pentagon UAP program called Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, or AATIP.'
DoD spokesperson Sue Gough responded to the Immaculate Constellation reporting with: 'The DOD has no record, present or historical, of any type of SAP called "IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION."'
Co-author Leslie Kean maintains a dated record of the article's publication on her own website under 16 December 2017.

Shellenberger's testimony sets out a Pentagon program timeline in which AAWSAP ran 2009-2017 with reports ending in 2010 but running through 2012 'according to the DOD,' the UAP Task Force ran 2020-2022, and AARO began in 2022 by order of Congress — a chronology that conflicts with the 2007-2012 AATIP dating in the NYT article and in the FAS account.

Luis Elizondo, the official the article identified as running the program, testified to Congress on 13 November 2024 that in his last position he 'managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council' and that 'the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies.'

Michael Gold testified in November 2024 that Lt. Commander Alex Dietrich's USS Nimitz encounter might have been 'lost to history' but for AAWSAP, tying the program the article exposed to the 2004 Nimitz case whose video the article helped make public.

entityDossier.denialPosture: The article itself records the Defense Department's position that the program was shut down in 2012, and simultaneously records that program backers say it continued — making the denial and its contradiction contemporaneous and jointly attributable. DoD's later flat denial of IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION, the program allegedly created in response to this article, is the second denial in the same chain.
connections: Luis Elizondo is the named program manager here and a sworn witness before House Oversight seven years later; the article is his standing credential.
Harry Reid appears as the program's political originator, connecting the article to the DIA solicitation, to BAASS, and to Nevada contracting.
The 38 Defense Intelligence Reference Documents released by DIA under FOIA in January 2019 are the article's documentary aftershock, and FAS explicitly links the two.
The article is the alleged causal trigger for IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION in 2017 per the whistleblower report entered into the record at the 13 November 2024 hearing.
It is the origin point for the sensor-data framing later adopted by ODNI's 2021 assessment, which describes UAP registering across radar, infrared, electro-optical and weapon seekers.
Co-author Leslie Kean later co-reported the David Grusch allegations, making her a through-line from 2017 disclosure to 2023 whistleblower testimony.

The unpublished 'records obtained by The New York Times' are a discrete, identifiable body of documents that no FOIA has surfaced and that would now fall within the scope of the NARA UAP Records Collection if they originated as government records.
openQuestions: What were the 'records obtained by The New York Times,' who provided them, and do copies exist in government custody subject to the NARA Record Group 615 transfer obligation?
Who were the 'backers' who said the program continued after 2012, and in what capacity did they continue investigating episodes?

Are AATIP and AAWSAP the same program, sequential programs, or a program and a successor portfolio? The NYT, FAS, DIA contracting records and Shellenberger's testimony give three incompatible date ranges.
Was the December 2017 disclosure an uncontrolled leak, or a sanctioned limited disclosure — and if the latter, who authorised it and what was it intended to protect?
Did any DoD component conduct a leak investigation following publication, and does a record of it exist?

entityDossier.whatItIs: 10 U.S.C. § 119, 'Special access programs: congressional oversight,' is the statute that governs how the Department of Defense must tell Congress about its special access programs. Enacted 4 December 1987 as section 1132(a)(1) of Public Law 100-180 and amended in 1990, 1996, 1999 and 2001, it requires an annual report on all SAPs, an annual report on each new SAP with justification, advance notice of classification changes, and — decisively — bars any SAP from being initiated until the defense committees have been notified and thirty days have elapsed. It also grants the Secretary of Defense a case-by-case waiver over the content of those reports.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the statute against which the concealment must be measured, and it is the statute a whistleblower report given to Congress in 2024 alleges is being deliberately circumvented. Subsection (f) is categorical: a special access program 'may not be initiated until' the defense committees are notified and thirty days pass. If a legacy retrieval or reverse-engineering effort exists as a DoD SAP and the defense committees were never notified, the illegality is not a matter of interpretation. Subsection (e) is the built-in escape hatch, letting the Secretary strip content from the reports on national-security grounds and narrow disclosure to twelve members. And the reporting obligations in subsections (a) and (b) were terminated outright effective 31 December 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328 — the annual SAP report to Congress simply stopped, in the same window in which the UAP Task Force was being stood up and AARO was being legislated. Michael Shellenberger's sworn testimony that an alleged UAP USAP is White-House-controlled and DoD-executed 'to avoid compliance with Title 10' is a claim about this section specifically.
entityDossier.narrative:
Section 119 was Congress's answer to the black-budget expansion of the 1980s. Enacted in the FY1988 defense authorisation, it imposed a reporting discipline on a category of program that by design resists reporting. Read as a whole, the section is a fairly aggressive assertion of legislative prerogative, and its subsequent amendment history shows Congress tightening it further: in 1990 Congress added subsection (f), the thirty-day pre-initiation notification bar, effective 1 October 1991, and rewrote subsection (c) to require fourteen days' advance notice of classification changes rather than thirty days' notice after the fact.

The reporting architecture has four parts. Under subsection (a), by 1 March each year the Secretary of Defense must submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP in that budget, a brief description, a brief discussion of major milestones, the actual cost for every prior fiscal year of the program, and the estimated total cost plus estimates for the current year, the budget year, and each of the four succeeding years. Under subsection (b), by 1 February each year the Secretary must report every new SAP with notice of the designation, justification for it, the current estimate of total program cost, and — a provision with real analytic teeth — 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.' That clause exists to stop the Department from hiding duplicate or successor programs under new names. Under subsection (c), any planned classification change or public declassification announcement requires a report to the defense committees not less than fourteen days beforehand, unless exceptional circumstances make that impossible.

Subsection (e) is the pressure valve. The Secretary 'may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report' if inclusion 'would adversely affect the national security,' with the waiver made on a case-by-case basis. When a waiver is used, the withheld information and the justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — that is, to twelve members across six bodies, and to nobody else. This is the statutory basis of what practitioners call a waived SAP. The implementing directive confirms the practice: access to waived SAPs is limited to the chairs, ranking minority members and staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise.

Subsection (f) is the hardest edge in the statute and the one most relevant to this board: 'A special access program may not be initiated until— (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' There is no waiver of subsection (f) in subsection (e) — the waiver reaches only (a), (b) and (c). Congress can, in principle, be denied the content of a report about a SAP. It cannot lawfully be denied notice that a DoD SAP is being initiated.

Which makes the terminating note in the current code text the most consequential single fact in this dossier. Under the heading 'Termination of Reporting Requirements,' the statute records: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.' The annual comprehensive SAP report and the annual new-SAP report both lapsed at the end of 2021, under a sunset written into the FY2017 NDAA. The pre-initiation notification in (f) survives. The routine, systematic, year-over-year visibility does not. Any analyst working this board should note the coincidence of timing: the UAP Task Force was established in August 2020, the ODNI preliminary assessment landed in June 2021, AARO was legislated in December 2021 and stood up in 2022, and the statutory obligation to give Congress an annual accounting of every DoD special access program expired on 31 December 2021.

The implementing machinery underneath the statute is set out in DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It establishes the Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary, a Senior Review Group, a Senior Working Group, and the DoD Special Access Program Central Office whose Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary and is the 'DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch.' Two provisions in it bear directly on the concealment argument. First, establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is 'by exception' and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. Second, and more starkly: 'No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' The contractor layer — precisely where a legacy program would sit — is prohibited by directive from talking to Congress about SAP material without permission from an office reporting to the Deputy Secretary of Defense. And the same directive designates USD(I&S), the office housing AARO, as the primary interface with ODNI for sharing compartmented capabilities into and out of DoD SAPs.

Witnesses have made the statutory argument directly. Tim Gallaudet told House Oversight in November 2024 that 'even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight' and that 'any and all past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs and activities are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress by preventing it from exercising its legislative and oversight responsibilities.' Shellenberger's source described the alleged workaround with unusual precision: the White House directs the Secretary of Defense to run the program, so it is executed by DoD but controlled by the White House. 'But that's the loophole.' Whether such a structure escapes subsection (f) turns on whether it is a special access program 'of the Department of Defense' — a question no court and no committee has resolved on the public record.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1) requires that 'not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs.'

10 U.S.C. 119(a)(2)(B) requires that for each special access program in the budget the report include a brief description, a brief discussion of major milestones, the actual cost for each prior fiscal year of the program, and the estimated total cost plus estimates for the current fiscal year, the budget year, and each of the four succeeding fiscal years.

10 U.S.C. 119(b) requires an annual report, not later than February 1, on each new special access program providing notice of the designation, justification for it, the current estimate of total program cost, and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.'

10 U.S.C. 119(c) requires the Secretary of Defense to report to the defense committees any planned change in the classification of a DoD special access program, or any planned declassification and public announcement, not less than 14 days beforehand, with a later-notice exception for 'exceptional circumstances' that must be explained in the report.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) permits the Secretary of Defense to waive any requirement under subsections (a), (b) or (c) that certain information be included in a report 'if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security,' with any such waiver made on a case-by-case basis.

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) provides that when a waiver is exercised, the withheld information and the justification for the waiver go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — twelve members in total.

10 U.S.C. 119(f) provides that 'a special access program may not be initiated until— (1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' The waiver authority in subsection (e) does not extend to subsection (f).

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Committee on Armed Services, the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate, and the corresponding committees and Subcommittee on Defense of the House.

The section was added by Public Law 100-180, division A, title XI, section 1132(a)(1), 4 December 1987, 101 Stat. 1151, and amended by Pub. L. 101-510 (1990), Pub. L. 104-106 (1996), Pub. L. 106-65 (1999) and Pub. L. 107-107 (2001).
Subsection (f), the 30-day pre-initiation notification bar, was added by Pub. L. 101-510, division A, title XIV, section 1482(a)(2), 5 November 1990, and took effect on 1 October 1991.

The statute carries a note headed 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' stating: 'For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328.' The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP report requirements therefore lapsed at the end of 2021.

DoD Directive 5205.07, effective 12 September 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, establishes the Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and provides that the Director, DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary and serves as the 'DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch, including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries.'

DoD Directive 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(g) provides that 'no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.'

DoD Directive 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(d) provides that 'establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments will be by exception' and that establishing SAPs to protect new and novel critical program information at any tier 'requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval.'

Michael Shellenberger testified on 13 November 2024 that a source told him an alleged UAP Unacknowledged Special Access Program 'is controlled by the White House and executed and administrated by the DOD to avoid compliance with Title 10 of the United States Code,' adding 'the White House directed the SECDEF to run it. But that's the loophole.'

Tim Gallaudet testified on 13 November 2024 that 'even the most sensitive Special Access Programs must be reported the Gang of Eight, and all compartmented programs must be reported to the Senate Intelligence Committee,' and that any past failures by DoD and IC components to report UAP programs 'are not only illegal but would have undermined Congress.'

entityDossier.denialPosture: There is no denial attached to the statute itself. The relevant absence is that no DoD component has ever publicly identified a UAP-related special access program in any section 119 report, and the annual reporting obligations that would have carried such an identification lapsed on 31 December 2021. The Department's only categorical statement in this area is Sue Gough's denial that any SAP named IMMACULATE CONSTELLATION appears in its records.
connections: Section 119(f)'s unwaivable 30-day pre-initiation notice is the specific legal provision the alleged White-House-directed, DoD-executed USAP structure is said to be engineered around.
Section 119(e)'s twelve-member disclosure floor is the statutory origin of the waived-SAP practice implemented through DoDD 5205.07, and is what Gallaudet means by 'Gang of Eight' reporting.

The 31 December 2021 termination of subsections (a) and (b) reporting, enacted by section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328 (FY2017 NDAA), coincides with the UAPTF-to-AARO transition and the enactment of 50 U.S.C. 3373 in December 2022.

DoDD 5205.07 places SAP governance under Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks as SAPOC chair and routes all congressional SAP contact through the DoD SAPCO Director, giving a single named office control over what Congress learns.

The contractor gag in DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1(g) directly implicates the defence-contractor layer this board is mapping: contractors cannot lawfully brief Congress on SAP material without DoD SAPCO approval, which structurally converts contractor whistleblowing into a security violation.

USD(I&S) is both the ODNI/IC interface under DoDD 5205.07 and the parent organisation of AARO, meaning the office Congress created to find unreported UAP programs sits inside the office that brokers compartmented sharing between the IC and DoD SAPs.

Luis Elizondo's testimony that he 'managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council' describes the same White-House-to-DoD execution pattern the Immaculate Constellation source alleges, from the inside.
